name: Sweden (since 1721)
summary: Sweden after the end of its empire in 1721: in union with Norway (1814–1905), neutral in both World Wars, and a welfare state.

knownFor.label: Carl Linnaeus
knownFor.note: Created the naming system for plants and animals.

knownFor.label: Allemansrätten
knownFor.note: Everyone’s right to roam in nature.

terrain.value: Forests and lakes such as Vänern and Vättern, farmland in the south (Skåne), and mountains and tundra in the north along the border with Norway.

climate.value: Cold winters and mild summers; the south is milder, and the far north lies above the Arctic Circle with very long winters.

resources.value: Iron ore from Kiruna and Bergslagen, timber from vast forests, and hydropower from northern rivers.

disasters.value: Famine in 1867–69 after crop failures, which drove many to emigrate; smallpox and cholera epidemics struck earlier.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural until the late 1800s; today over 85% live in towns, mainly Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö.

disease.value: Smallpox vaccination from 1816 and later public health reforms gave Sweden one of the world’s longest life expectancies.

migration.value: About 1.3 million emigrated to America (1850–1930); immigration later.

economicBase.value: Iron and timber, then industry; the largest companies include Volvo, Ericsson and Vattenfall.

tradeRoutes.value: Exports of iron, timber and paper, later cars and machines, through ports such as Gothenburg, and trade within the EU from 1995.

wealth.value: Poor in the 1800s, it became one of the richest countries in the world by the mid-1900s through industry.

moneyAndTax.value: The krona, introduced in 1873 with the Scandinavian Monetary Union; high taxes fund the welfare state.

inequality.value: Among the lowest income inequality in the world since the mid-1900s through taxes and welfare, though gaps have grown since the 1990s.

governmentType.value: A unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy: King Carl XVI Gustaf is only ceremonial, and under the 1974 Instrument of Government he has no formal political power.

keyRulers.value: Charles XIV John (the French marshal Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte), who founded the House of Bernadotte in 1818.

succession.value: The crown passes in the Bernadotte family (to the eldest child regardless of sex since 1980); governments are formed after Riksdag elections.

institutions.value: The Riksdag (parliament), single-chamber since 1971, the government, the courts and the parliamentary ombudsman (1809).

stability.value: A stable constitutional state since the 1809 Instrument of Government; peaceful reforms brought full democracy by 1921.

eliteConflict.value: The Hats and Caps parties competed in the Age of Liberty (1719–72) until Gustav III seized power in 1772; later, coalition politics.

armyAndTech.value: Neutral for two centuries; joined NATO in 2024.

majorWars.value: Officially neutral in both world wars and non-aligned through the Cold War until 2022; joined the EU on 1 January 1995 and NATO on 7 March 2024. The “last war 1814” claim is not in the part read.

territoryChange.value: Lost Finland, its eastern half, to Russia in 1809.

inventions.value: Dynamite, the safety match, the three-point seatbelt, Spotify.

scienceEducation.value: Carl Linnaeus at Uppsala and the Royal Academy of Sciences (1739); compulsory schooling from 1842 and the Nobel Prizes from 1901.

openness.value: Open to trade, ideas and immigration, and a member of the EU since 1995, though neutral in both World Wars.

communicationTransport.value: The Göta Canal (1832), railways from the 1850s, Stockholm’s metro (1950) and the Öresund Bridge to Denmark (2000).

religion.value: The Church of Sweden was confirmed as Lutheran by the Uppsala Synod of 1593. Its present share of the population and the separation of church and state in 2000 are not covered in the part read.

languageWriting.value: Swedish; Sámi, Finnish, Meänkieli, Romani and Yiddish have been official minority languages since 2000.

artsArchitecture.value: Writers such as August Strindberg and Astrid Lindgren.

socialStructure.value: Once a society of nobles, clergy, burghers and peasants (the four estates of the Riksdag until 1866); now a large middle class.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong identity built on the folkhem (“people’s home”) welfare state, neutrality, and traditions such as Midsummer.

dailyLife.value: Wooden houses and flats; meatballs, fish.

ideasReligions.value: Lutheranism, Enlightenment science, popular movements (temperance, free churches, labour) and social democracy from the 1930s.

peakPeriod.value: The post-war decades (about 1945–75), when industry boomed and the welfare state grew under Social Democratic governments.

declineSignals.value: No decline of the modern state; its biggest setbacks were losing Finland to Russia in 1809 and a severe banking crisis in the early 1990s.

outcome.value: Still in existence as a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy.
